extracted.intended_audience: Owners, managers, designers, contractors, and city agencies responsible for large buildings and building projects in New York City (building professionals and compliance officers).
extracted.subtask_description: Summary of New York City local laws, rules, and executive orders that set mandatory requirements for building energy performance, benchmarking, audits, retro-commissioning, lighting, sub-metering, and use of green-building and geothermal screening tools for city-owned projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Law 86 (LL86) — green building requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Law 86 of 2005 (LL86) — adopted to implement green building goals and policies for covered projects; rules were published and finalized after public comment and hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law was developed by the Administration with the City Council; Rules for LL86 were published in draft on Dec 1, 2006, went through public comment/hearing and became effective April 2, 2007. LL86 establishes that projects must comply with the green building rating system selected in the LL86 Rules (see related entry for the 2009 amendment selecting LEED®).

rubrics_metrics.name: LL86 Rules — selected green building rating system (June 21, 2009 amendment)
rubrics_metrics.description: June 21, 2009 amendment to the LL86 Rules redefines the selected green building rating system as the Version 3 LEED® 2009 suite of systems (the most recent version published by USGBC at that time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments to the LL86 Rules occur following CAPA public comment and hearing. Executive Order 149 (see below) authorizes periodic evaluation and rule amendments to increase stringency as the green building industry develops.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 149 — Director authority on LL86 implementation
rubrics_metrics.description: Executive Order 149 (June 27, 2011) gives the Mayor and Director authority regarding implementation of LL86, including expanding categories of projects subject to the law's goals and policies and periodically evaluating and making the law's minimum requirements more stringent by amending the LL86 Rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director may expand project categories, evaluate stringency of minimum requirements, and issue amendments to LL86 Rules as warranted by industry developments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Law 84 (LL84) — annual benchmarking and public disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Law 84 requires annual benchmarking data to be submitted by owners of buildings with more than 50,000 square feet for public disclosure by May 1 each year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benchmarking brings transparency for energy and water usage and informs building owners and tenants on how to make their buildings more efficient. The Department of Buildings has published a Benchmarking Rule that provides details on how to benchmark to comply with LL84.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Law 85 / NYCECC — energy code for renovations and alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Law 85 (part of the New York City Energy Conservation Code, NYCECC) requires buildings to meet the most current energy code for any renovation or alteration project; renovations are no longer exempt simply because they affect less than half of the building system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NYCECC currently comprises the 2010 Energy Conservation Construction Code of New York State (ECCCNYS), Local Law 85 of 2009, Local Law 48 of 2010 and Local Law 1 of 2011. For updates to NYCECC, consult the City's Energy Code page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Law 87 (LL87) — energy audits and retro-commissioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Law 87 requires large buildings to perform energy audits, conduct retro-commissioning where appropriate, and submit audit and retro-commissioning information to the City.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required submittals include: basic team information; general building information; existing equipment inventory; energy end use breakdown; energy conservation measures identified from the audit; and retro-commissioning measures. LL87 aligns with annual benchmarking to help optimize buildings' energy performance. The Department of Buildings has published a rule giving more detail on how to perform audits and retro-commissioning to comply with LL87.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Law 88 (LL88) — lighting upgrades and tenant sub-metering
rubrics_metrics.description: Local Law 88 requires large non-residential buildings to upgrade lighting to meet current New York City Energy Conservation Code standards, and to install electrical sub-meters for each large non-residential tenant space and provide monthly energy statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: LL88 applies to large non-residential buildings; lighting must meet current NYCECC standards and tenant-level electrical usage must be sub-metered with monthly statements provided to tenants. See the detailed summary and rule text for compliance thresholds and timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local Law 6 of 2016 — geothermal screening for city-owned projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to Local Law 6 of 2016, the Mayor’s Office of Sustainability and the NYC Department of Design and Construction developed an online screening tool to help identify areas where geothermal heat pump systems may be an option for retrofitting buildings’ heating and cooling systems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tool evaluates closed loop, open loop, and standing column well systems. City agencies are required to use the screening tool in planning new construction of city-owned buildings and retrofitting existing city-owned buildings' heating and cooling systems. On sites where geothermal systems are geologically and technically suitable, the annual social cost of carbon savings is calculated based on projected carbon footprint reduction. See Local Law 6 of 2016 and the geothermal tool for details.
